name: Together AI GPU Clusters (HGX H100, on-demand)
region: not stated on the pricing page
price_basis: per GPU-hour - the page states 'All prices per gpu per hour'. On-demand pay-as-you-go: NVIDIA HGX H100 $5.49; HGX B200 $8.99. H200, B300, GB200 NVL72 and GB300 NVL72 are 'Contact us' on-demand. Every Reserved tier is 'Contact sales'. Fetched 2026-10-03. PRICE CLASS: this is a PUBLISHED LIST PRICE - an asking rate a new customer is quoted, not a realised, discounted or negotiated transaction rate. A real bill is at or below this and typically well below it once commitments, credits and committed-use discounts are applied.
notes:
A NARROW RECORD BY DESIGN: Together publishes exactly one number, $5.49 per H100-hour, and gates everything else - H200, B300, GB200, GB300, and every reservation - behind a sales conversation. Recording it is still worth it because $5.49 lands in the interesting middle band: cheaper than every hyperscaler on-demand H100 (AWS $6.88, GCP $11.06, Azure $12.29), dearer than Runpod's in-stock $3.49 and Lambda's $3.99. It is also the only provider here whose headline H100 number is not undercut by a cheaper in-stock alternative, which makes it a candidate if you want a managed inference platform with the GPUs attached rather than bare compute. Do NOT confuse this with Together's per-token serverless prices on the same page - those are a different unit entirely and are not a supply figure. They have also announced on-demand B200s on GPU Clusters, which the $8.99 reflects.

 EXPORT CONTROL (2026-10-04, mechanism-level; sources spl-bis-2026-05-d5-guidance, spl-bis-2026-01-advanced-computing-case-by-case): renting capacity does NOT remove the export-control question, it relocates it. Providing remote access to controlled computing capability can constitute a transfer under the EAR, so the provider must screen the end user; and separately, under the 91 FR 1684 licence regime the consignee must run KYC procedures to prevent unauthorized remote access and must manage and limit IaaS access to the hardware - obligations pushed onto the customer, who must be told to implement them. For a customer headquartered or parented in Country Group D:5 or Macau the 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A) end-user/parent test can bite even when the capacity is consumed in a permitted region. Recorded true because the underlying hardware is controlled and the provider carries the screening duty, not because access to a US region is itself restricted.

 LEAD TIME: null, and correct as null. For a listed on-demand instance type the provisioning delay is effectively zero - capacity is allocated per request - so a week count would be meaningless; the real gate for scarce shapes is either a quota increase or a capacity reservation, not a lead time. Where a published commitment horizon exists it IS recorded: AWS documents that a Capacity Block may be reserved with a start time up to EIGHT WEEKS in the future (source spl-aws-capacity-block-booking-horizon), which is a floor on how far ahead scarce capacity must be committed, not a wait. On-demand and Spot tiers publish no lead time at all; their constraint is availability, and the repo records that as availability=in-stock or a spot/reality note rather than as a fabricated week figure. Probe log in source spl-negative-no-oem-publishes-lead-time.
